Under Austrian procedural law a successful complainant is not a party to the penal procedure, when a penalty under the GDPR is imposed.

The HDPA imposed a EUR 5,000 fine on the biggest electric power company in Greece because it did not respond to data subject's right to access. The HDPA highlighted that even when the data controller does not keep any record of the data subject's personal data, it should notify the data subject of its inability to respond to the access request according to Article 12(4) GDPR.
The AEPD fined €1,500 a data controller for the lack of a privacy policy on its website, under Article 13 GDPR.

The President of the Personal Data Protection Office of Poland (PUODO) imposed a fine of €4,700 (PLN 20,000) on a primary school for unlawful processing of children's biometric data when using the school canteen.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion regarding the processing of data in the context of a life insurance policy. It recalled several provisions of the Slovenian Insurance Act (ZZavar) and found that insurance companies may have a proper legal basis for the processing of personal data in specific databases if the companies fulfill the requirements provided for in ZZavar. It also noted that in the context of a non-binding opinion the IP cannot determine whether in a particular case these requirements are fulfilled.
The ANSPDCP fined association EUR. 2,000 because it did not respond to its order to provide information and to allow access to personal data as required by Article 58(1)(a) and (e).

A municipal employee complained that the Comune di Urago d'Oglio had published on its website a document and the full text of a court judgment containing her personal data, including health data. The Garante found there was no legal basis for the publication, that it breached the principles of lawfulness and minimisation, and that it violated the ban on disseminating health data. The municipality's arguments (implicit consent, Article 52 of the Code, transparency) were rejected. The Garante imposed a fine of EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website; no corrective measures were needed since the data had been removed.
<!--Here the main article starts-->The Danish Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) issued a reprimand concerning the requirements for consent as required by Article 6(1)(a) GDPR.

The ANSPDCP fined Vodafone România SA 3,000 € for failing to implement adequate technical and organisational measures when processing personal data, thus violating the principles of accuracy, integrity, confidentiality and accountability.

The ICO imposed a fine (monetary penalty) of GBP 500,000 on Cathay Pacific Airways Limited (“Cathay Pacific”), for failing to protect the security of its customers’ personal data. Respective investigation that led to said fine, was started on October 25th, 2018, after Cathay Pacific self-reported the data breaches in violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR. Between October 2014 and May 2018 Cathay Pacific’s computer systems lacked appropriate security measures which led to customers’ personal data being exposed, 111,578 of whom were from the UK, and approximately 9.4 million more worldwide.

A woman complained about a segment of the TV programme 'Le Iene' in which she was interviewed, face obscured, by someone posing as a client, and her real voice and personal details were broadcast and put online, making her identifiable. The Garante found the processing unlawful as it breached the fairness and lawfulness principle and the journalistic code of conduct, including the rules on sexual-sphere data. It fined RTI EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The video had already been removed during the investigation, and the claim for compensation was held to be outside its competence.
Luxembourg DPA argues it cannot proceed and is not willing to open an investigation against a company established abroad that has not designated an EU Represenative.
The AEPD imposed a 1.500 € fine against a cafeteria which placed surveillance cameras outside its establishment on a public space and thus, violated the principle of data minimisation.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion as foreseen under Article 58(3) GDPR regarding spamming e-mails to Slovenian company, which were sent by a travel agency without any prior registration.
Following an investigation the Spanish Data Protection Authority imposed a fine of EUR 60,000 on XFERA MÓVILES for violation of Article 6(1)(a) GDPR.

A woman complained to the AEPD that Vodafone España billed her for a phone line she says she never contracted, and Vodafone did not answer the Agency's information requests. The AEPD opened a sanction procedure for processing her data without a legal basis (Article 6.1 GDPR) and proposed a fine of EUR 100,000. Vodafone paid EUR 60,000 on 24 December 2019, using both 20% reductions (acknowledging responsibility and voluntary payment). The AEPD therefore closed the procedure under Article 85 of Law 39/2015.

Following an investigation the AEPD imposed a fine of 20.000 EUR on IBERIA Airlines for the violation of Article 6(1)(f) GDPR, when further sending unsolicited emails after a customer has requested the deletion of his data.

The Spanish AEPD closed proceedings PS/00292/2019 after the respondent paid voluntarily. The respondent had posted a fake adult-contact advert on a website using the complainant's photo, name, phone number and sexual descriptions, created from an IP address linked to a company. The proposed fine was EUR 1,000 for infringing Article 6(1) GDPR; a 20% reduction for voluntary payment brought it to EUR 800, which was paid on 16 January 2020. The payment waived administrative appeals.

The ICO decided that Devon and Cornwall Police rightly refused to disclose information about the death of a man with mental health issues who had been restrained with an emergency response belt while in police custody. It considered the information personal data and it found that disclosure would be generally unlawful, since the admitted legal basis of legitimate interest is not sufficient to outweigh the data subject’s fundamental rights and freedoms.

The Estonian Data Protection Authority (AKI) ruled that the access to public information may be lawfully restricted when the documents requested are not finalised. A non signed environmental impact assessment drafted by the Ministry of Environment falls under this restriction.

On the 31st January 2020 the Information Commissioners Office (ICO) supported the position of the City of York Council, finding that details of the Council's employees professional qualifications amounted to personal information. As such, the City of York Council were correct in applying the Section 40(2) Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA) exemption.

A private individual reported to the Garante that the municipality of Colledara had published on its website full lists and records of a public recruitment competition, including names, birth data, scores and oral exam questions of candidates, including those excluded or not successful. The municipality removed the documents and argued that the call for applications and candidates' acceptance of it justified publication. The Garante held that no law or regulation provided a legal basis for such dissemination, that consent cannot serve as a basis for public bodies, and that the principles of lawfulness and data minimisation were breached. It fined the municipality EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website; no corrective measures were imposed since the conduct had ceased.

A hospital in Verona notified the Garante of three personal data breaches found in its own periodic audits: staff had improperly accessed the electronic health records (dossier sanitario) of 16 patients who were also hospital colleagues, out of curiosity, and in some cases by using a colleague's unattended logged-in workstation. The Garante found that the hospital's technical and organisational measures did not adequately limit access to treating staff, in breach of Art. 5(1)(f) GDPR. It ordered the hospital to complete the access-control measures within 90 days and fined it EUR 30,000. The decision is to be published in full on the Garante's website.

<!--Here the main article starts--> On December 2020, 23rd the Italian Data Protection Authority imposed a fine of 30 000 Euro on the university of Rome “la Sapienza”, acting as a data controller under the GDPR. The data controller did not process personal data with an appropriate level of security, as required by article 32, read in conjunction with article 33 GDPR.

With the provision No. 10 of 23 january 2020, the Italian Data Protection Authority assessed Istat's request for authorization to process data, pursuant to article 2-quinquiesdecies of the Privacy Code (Legislative Decree 196/2003).

The Garante received several hundred complaints and reports about unwanted promotional calls made for TIM, and TIM also sent a series of data breach notifications. After inspections at TIM and at its marketing partners, it found many violations in TIM's marketing: calls without consent, poorly managed opt-out lists, objections to marketing not respected, forced consent in the TIM Party programme and in apps and paper forms, long retention of data of other operators' customers, and poor breach and data-accuracy management. It imposed a single fine of EUR 27,802,946, set at 0.2% of TIM's turnover. It also ordered a permanent restriction of certain processing, a series of corrective measures and publication of the decision.

A man complained that the municipality of Francavilla Fontana had published on its online official notice board a determination on legal costs that contained details of his health conditions linked to service, and the full IBAN of the lawyer hired by the municipality. The Garante found the publication unlawful, as health data may not be disseminated and the IBAN went beyond what was necessary. The municipality had said it was a clerical error, had removed the document and described measures taken. It did not reply to the notice of violations. The Garante fined the municipality EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Estonian DPA (AKI) ruled that any settlement of claims between data controller and data subject does not deprive the latter of the possibility to exercise their right of access according to Article 15 GDPR, regardless of the fact that the data controller is a public or private entity.
Vodafone has been fined € 44.000 for accidentally disclosing personal data to a third party.

The Bulgarian Commission for Personal Data Protection (CPDP) imposed a fine of BGN 10,000 (approximately EUR 5,000) on a company providing utility services. The data controller processed personal data without any legal basis as required by Article 6(1) GDPR.
The HDPA rejected complaint filed by alien with regard to the erasure of his data from the Schengen Information System (SIS) and the National Register of Undesirable Aliens (EKANA).

The HPDA found that a Nautical Club unlawfully processed biometric data via an access control system and failed to conduct a DPIA, imposed €56,000 in fines, and ordered suspension of processing until a DPIA is completed.
The Persónuvernd found that a telecommunication company sent unauthorised marketing emails; despite the data subject’s objection violated the GDPR and the ePrivacy Directive.

The HDPA issued EUR 150,000 fine against Greek supplier of marine bunker fuels and lubricants for violations of the principles of lawfulness, fairness and transparency and the security of processing according to the GDPR, while carrying out data processing operations in computer infrastructures (server hardware and software).
The data protection authority had to weigh up the right to secrecy against the right to freedom of expression.
The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) fined the defendant € 15000 for cookies placed without prior consent.

The Romanian authority concluded an investigation of an energy supplier on 16 December 2019. It found that the company processed a complainant's data unlawfully, being unable to prove consent to send notifications to his email address, and without respecting accuracy. The company also did not stop the notifications although the complainant objected several times. Two administrative fines of 14,334.30 lei each (about EUR 3,000 each) were imposed, and the company has paid them.

Romania's data protection authority concluded an investigation on 13 December 2019 into a shipping and trading company, following a complaint about audio-video cameras in offices and changing rooms, fingerprint access control, and use of a former employee's identity in work emails. It found four sets of infringements. It issued two warnings (for failing to inform data subjects, and for unlawfully using a former employee's data in emails) and two fines of RON 23,893 (about EUR 5,000) each, for excessive video surveillance of employees and for processing biometric fingerprint data when less intrusive means were available. It also ordered corrective measures on information, data minimisation in video monitoring and access control, and security policies.

Following a complaint, the Romanian DPA investigated a company and closed the investigation on 13 December 2019. It found excessive video surveillance of employees in offices and changing areas, processing of employees' fingerprints, inadequate information to data subjects, and unlawful use of a former employee's data in emails. It issued two fines of RON 23,893 (EUR 5,000 each) and two warnings, plus corrective measures on transparency, data minimisation and security.

A former hospital director complained that the hospital's successor institution kept archived copies of his work e-mail accounts, which he had been allowed to use privately, and searched them for a document without telling him. The authority upheld the complaint. It found breaches of storage limitation, fairness, purpose limitation and lawful basis. It also found, of its own motion, a breach of accountability and transparency. It banned storage of the private correspondence, ordered a review and deletion, and ordered internal rules and information for staff on e-mail archiving and searches. It fined the institution HUF 500,000 and ordered the authority to pay the complainant HUF 10,000 for exceeding the processing deadline.

The Garante investigated Eni Gas e Luce after dozens of complaints about promotional calls made without consent, after opt-outs, or to numbers on the public opposition register. An inspection in February 2019 showed systemic problems in the company's telemarketing and teleselling: no checks on consent in lists bought from list providers, consent refusals not respected, late updating of blacklists, over-long data retention, and poor cooperation with the authority. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, imposed corrective orders and a fine of EUR 8,500,000, set at 5% of the statutory maximum of EUR 171.16 million, and ordered publication of the decision.

Several people complained to the Italian DPA that Eni Gas e Luce had signed energy supply contracts they never requested, often with wrong personal data, through door-to-door sales agencies. After inspections in February 2019, the Garante found that Eni's organisational and technical controls over its agencies were inadequate, so inaccurate data were processed (about 7,200 customers affected) in breach of the fairness, accuracy, integrity and accountability principles. It ordered Eni to bring its processes into line within six months, permanently restricted further processing of the data of the 7,200 customers, and fined it EUR 3,000,000, with publication of the decision.
The HDPA issued a reprimand to the Ministry of Mercantile Marine and Island Policy for infringement of the right of access.

A BfDI press release announces two fines. This record concerns the smaller one: Rapidata GmbH, a telecoms provider, was fined EUR 10,000 because it failed to appoint a data protection officer despite being asked several times. The amount took into account that the company is a micro-enterprise. The same press release also covers a EUR 9,550,000 fine against 1&1 Telecom GmbH under Article 32, which is not part of this record.

The Dutch DPA received a tip in July 2018 that a company obliged its employees to scan their fingerprints to clock in and out. After an ex officio investigation with unannounced visits in November 2018 and March 2019, it found that the company processed employees' biometric data from 25 May 2018 to 16 April 2019 without a valid exception under Article 9(2) GDPR (neither explicit consent nor the UAVG authentication/security exception). It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 725,000, which is the base fine of category IV under its 2019 fine policy rules, with no increase or decrease. It rejected the company's arguments that a reprimand would suffice and that it relied on its supplier.

The Austrian Data Protection Authority (DSB) held that a Swiss based company violated Articles 13 and 14 GDPR by not providing all information required in the email sent for its newsletter subscription to the complainant and even failed to provide such information later, in the course of the proceeding before the DSB.
A mayor used citizen's data to send letters for his re-election campaign. The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) issued a warning and a fine of € 5000 for violation of the principle of purpose limitation.

A former client of a veterinarian complained that the vet, who was a municipal election candidate and outgoing alderman, used his client file to send electoral propaganda letters. The inspection service found that the vet admitted using the client list, 654 people, for the mailing. The Litigation Chamber held this was further processing incompatible with the original purpose, in breach of Articles 5(1)(b) and 6(4) GDPR. It imposed a reprimand and an administrative fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision in anonymised form.
The ANSPDCP fined € 11.000 Fan Courrier Express SRL for violations of f Article 32 paragraphs (1) and (2) GDPR.
The ANSDPC in Romania fined BNP Paribas because it did not respond to the applicant’s access request within the one-month period required under Article 12(3) GDPR.
The French DPA (CNIL) imposed a fine of €500,000 for marketing solicitations which violate the GDPR.

The Persónuvernd decided that the transmission of employee’s call record to his ex-wife violates the national act on electronic monitoring and processing of personal information generated by electronic monitoring.

The Persónuvernd decided that the transmission of employee’s call record to his ex-wife violates the national act on electronic monitoring and processing of personal information generated by electronic monitoring.
The NAIH confirmed that the exercice of the access right and the accuracy principle do not require to provide certified copies to the data subject.

The Hungarian DPA (NAIH) fined a controller 1 million HUF (approximately 2,830 EUR), and ordered the deletion of data from the initiative "Join the EPPO", for the processing of personal data with no legal basis and for the failing to provide data subjects with adequate information on all relevant circumstances of the processing.
The AEPD imposed a fine of € 3,000 against the General Labour Union (GCT) for the violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.
The Ministry of Internal Affairs has been ordered to ensure a sufficient level of security regarding the personal data collected by automatic speed camera.
The AEPD imposed a fine of € 900 to Todotecnicos24h S.L for violation of Article 13 GDPR.
The ICO issued a decision on the necessity of a disclosure of information hold by a public entity to satisfy the legitimate public interests of accountability and transparency.
The AEPD approved Centros comerciales Carrefour S.A compliance with the GDPR after having used its investigation powers.
The AEPD approved a transport hub's compliance with Articles 32 and 33 GDPR after having used its investigation powers.
The AEPD confirmed an online pharmacy's (Promofarma ecom S.L) compliance with the GDPR after having used its investigation powers.
The AEPD held that an outdated privacy policy on a webpage violates Article 13 GDPR.

The Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL) followed the measures implemented by BOUTIQUE.AERO to prevent the excessive video surveillance of its employees and found that the controller was compliant with the GDPR. The CNIL closed the case.
The IP issued an advisory opinion on the principle of data minimisation and on the processing which is necessary for the performance of a contract in the banking sector.
The AEPD found that the El Maestro Cerrajero SL’s privacy policy complied with Article 13 GDPR, after the page was updated by the controller during the procedure.
The DPA ordered a bank (KUTXABANK S.A.) to respond to a subject access request.
On 4 November 2019, the Slovenian DPA (IP) exercised its powers under Article 58(3) GDPR to issue an advisory opinion regarding requirements for a consent.
On 4 November 2019, the Slovenian DPA (IP) exercised its powers under Article 58(3) GDPR to issue an advisory opinion regarding processor's and controller's roles.
The AKI re-examined complaint about financial service provider’s incomplete response to data subject’s access request after appeal.

13 November: The DPA re-examined complaint about financial service provider’s incomplete response to data subject’s access request after appeal The DPA examined appeal against its decision, with which it had closed a case against the financial service provider Luminor Pank AS. The appellant complained that the company, in response to his access request, provided an incomplete dataset in English. The DPA found that much of the data that the complainant found as missing is data that the complainant is expected to possess. So, it concluded that the company is not obliged to provide data that the data subject already possesses under Articles 13(4) and 14(5) GDPR. Thus, the DPA found that the company has adequately fulfilled the obligation to inform the data subject of the data processing as required by Articles 13-15 GDPR. Finally, the DPA pointed out that the complainant had indicated in its customer profile a language preference to use English, which justifies the data export in English (Article 12(1) GDPR).
The Commissioner ruled that complaints about a property were the complainant's personal data and applied Regulation 5(3) of the EIR to prevent disclosure,
The ICO issued a decision, regarding disclosure of information which do not include personal data Category:2019
The ICO issued a decision regarding the refusal to access to third party personal data.
Category:2019 Category:Article 12(5) GDPR The ICO issued a decisions regarding refusal to access to third party personal data.

This is not the decision itself but the authority's 2020 annual report, which briefly mentions the case. In November 2019 the Baden-Württemberg data protection authority fined a restaurant EUR 5,000 for extensive video surveillance with 24 cameras and 350 seats. The authority found the surveillance was not necessary to protect the controller's interests, since the stated reasons (protecting the buffet from poisoning by competitors) were not backed by facts or general experience. The report calls it a serious case of unlawful video surveillance. No formal reasoning, reference number or exact date is given.
The AEPD imposed a fine of € 6.000 for unlawful processing data from a public registry without a legal basis under Article 6 GDPR.
The Persónuvernd issued a decision on the disclosure of personal data to third party in the context of a recruitment process in line with Article 5(1) GDPR principles.

The Berlin data protection commissioner issued a fine of about EUR 14.5 million against the real estate company Deutsche Wohnen SE. On-site inspections in 2017 and 2019 found that tenants' personal data was kept in an archive system with no way of deleting data no longer needed, so years-old private and financial data was still stored. The company had been urgently advised in 2017 to change the system but had not fixed it by March 2019. The authority also imposed further fines of EUR 6,000–17,000 for 15 individual cases of unlawful storage. The decision was not yet final and could be challenged.
ICO issued a decision regarding access to third party personal data.
The Maltese supervisory authority fined a bank €8000 for failing to respond to an access request.
The HDPA rejected appeal filed by the Greek bank Eurobank Ergasias S.A. against HDPA's older decision linked to the exercise of the right to access and right to object under GDPR.

A member of parliament's scanned hospital access request form, sent only to the Military Hospital, appeared in news articles in February 2019. The authority found that the hospital did not notify the breach within 72 hours and did not record it in its breach register. It also found that the hospital had no internal incident-handling policy when the breach occurred, which meant inadequate organisational security measures. The authority imposed a fine of HUF 2,500,000 and ordered publication of the decision with the controller's identification data.

The LfDI (Baden-Württemberg) imposed a fine of EUR 100,000 on an medium-sized food craft company. The data controller unlawfully processed personal data and violated Article 5(1)(f) GDPR. It also did not process personal data with an appropriate level of security, as required by Article 32 GDPR.
The Spanish DAP ordered Google to delist an article based on the "right to be forgotten".

The HDPA imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 and a reprimand to the telecommunication company Wind Hellas for violation of the GDPR and of the national law implementing the ePrivacy Directive and it issued a reprimand to the telephone services company ΠΛΕΓΜΑ ΝΕΤ for violation of the GDPR.
The UODO imposed the first fine on a public entity for unlawful processing of personal data in the Public Information Bulletin (BIP).
The UODO imposed a fine of ca €47,000 on a limited liability company ClickQuickNow Sp. z o. o. for preventing the exercise of the right to withdraw consent. Category:Article 5(1)(a) GDPR

The ANSPDCP fined € 2.000 Vodafone România S.A. for violations of Article 13(1) Law no. 506/2004, read in conjunction with Article 13(5) of the same Law no. 506/2004 implementing the ePrivacy Directive.
The Commissioner fined a doctor € 14,000 for publishing sensitive patient data on Instagram.

A fine of NOK 1,200,000 (approximately €120,000), reduced from NOK 2,000,000, was imposed against the Education Agency of the Municipality of Oslo due to breach of personal data security in the mobile application “Skolemelding”. The fine was issued due to the application's lack of security and subsequent violations of Article 32(1)(b) GDPR and Article 32(1)(d) GDPR and of the principle of accountability as foreseen in Article 5(2) GDPR read in conjunction with Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.
<!--Here the main article starts--> The DSB found an Article 32 GDPR violation where a dating platform did not require a double opt-in confirmation for email addresses used in the sign-up process.
The HDPA re-examined complaints against the Greek internet and telecommunications service provider Forthnet.gr upon appeal and decided to reduce the fine it had previously imposed on it.

The Spanish DPA fined the airline Vueling €18,000 for relying on pre-checked consent boxes that enabled non-essential cookies and for continuing to use non-essential cookies even after users clicked "reject all."
The ANSPDCP finalised two investigations at Raiffeisen Bank S.A. and Vreau Credit S.R.L. and fined the two data controllers for violation of Article 32(1), (2) and (4) GDPR.

A person complained about the security cameras operated in the Kerepes town hall building, including the lack of prior information. The Authority extended the procedure ex officio to the municipality's general camera practice. It found that the camera surveillance breached the GDPR, that no information was given to data subjects before 26 March 2019, and that in the earlier period there was no designated controller, internal policy or privacy notice. It banned the unlawful camera processing and fined the municipality HUF 5,000,000, partly upholding the complaint. It also ordered publication of the decision and awarded the complainant HUF 10,000 for exceeding the procedural deadline.
The Rhineland-Palatinate DPA (LfDI) fined a local hospital € 105.000 due to its deficient organisational and structural personal data processing system.

Romania's data protection authority finished an investigation at Inteligo Media SA on 26 September 2019. On the avocatnet.ro website, the box for the daily 'Personal Update' email was left unticked, with text that the user ticks only to opt out, so users who did nothing were subscribed automatically. The company could not prove explicit consent for 4,357 users and relied on an inappropriate legal basis ('performance of a contract') for the daily email. The authority found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (b), 6(1)(a) and 7 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 9,000.
The APD/GBA issued a warning because a controller did not delete personal data at request, following job application process.
The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) fined € 10000 for requiring an ID to issue a new loyalty card, which violated the principle of data minimisation.
The Polish DPA (UODO) find the company Morele.net €660000 for violating the principle of data confidentiality and failing to ensure the security and confidentiality of personal data processed.

With the aim of ensuring the supremacy of EU law, the Portuguese DPA 'disapplied' several provisions of Portuguese Law 58/2019 in light of the GDPR's coming into force. It found that the disapplied articles jeopardised the application of the GDPR.

The DPA interpreted Article 44(2) of Law 58/2019 as conferring a discretionary power to assess, in cases where a GDPR violation is established, whether it is justified to depart from the legal rule of imposing a financial penalty on a given public body. The CNPD took the view that the waiver provided for in Article 44 can only be requested by public bodies and decided upon after notification of the accusation of an administrative offence, in the context of a specific administrative offence procedure.

The DVI director decided on 26 August 2019 to fine an online shop operator EUR 7,000. A person had repeatedly asked the company in 2018 to erase their data, including their mobile number, but the company kept sending commercial text messages to that number. The company also answered the person late, did not cooperate with the DVI, supplied information late and did not comply with the DVI's order. The company may appeal to court within ten working days.

In August 2019 the Berlin data protection commissioner imposed fines on Delivery Hero Germany GmbH totalling EUR 195,407, fees included. The fines were set in two notices, because some of the breaches fell under the data protection law in force before the GDPR; the press release gives no amount for each notice. Most of the cases concerned disregard of data subject rights: accounts of former customers were not deleted (ten cases), advertising emails were sent despite objections, and access requests were not answered or answered late (five cases). The authority concluded that the repeated breaches pointed to structural organisational problems. The new owner Takeaway.com accepted the notices and did not appeal, so the decision is final. The source is the commissioner's press release of 19 September 2019, not the notices themselves.

The Dutch DPA (AP) after investigation found multiple violations and decided to fine the Credit Registration Office (BKR) €830.000, because it charged fees for digital access requests and limited free access requests per mail to one per year. The BKR has announced they will appeal the fine. Additionally the BKR requested the AP does not publish their decision, but the Arhem court declined and the AP has published their decision.

The Austrian DPA stated that the right to access does not always apply in absolute terms and that it may be restricted by third-party interests such as secrecy obligations. However, in order for such a restriction to apply, a data controller must properly substantiate their arguments for denying the right to access.

Two judges complained that the president of the Budapest Environs Regional Court compiled a list of judges who were members of the Hungarian Judges' Association, taken from payroll membership-fee deductions and including tax IDs, and handed it out at a managers' meeting on 22 February 2019. The authority found the court unlawfully processed the data in breach of purpose limitation (Art. 5(1)(b)) and Art. 6 GDPR. It ordered the court to notify meeting participants that the data must be deleted, and imposed a fine of HUF 3,000,000 on its own initiative, rejecting the complainants' request for a fine as they had no standing on that point. The decision is to be published with the court's identifying data.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation on 2 July 2019 into a hotel operator, World Trade Center Bucharest. A printed breakfast check-in list with personal data of 46 guests was photographed by unauthorised outsiders and the data was published online. The authority found a breach of Article 32 GDPR, because the controller had not made sure staff only process data on its instructions and had not applied adequate technical and organisational measures. It imposed a fine of 71,028 lei, equal to EUR 15,000. The investigation began after the controller's own breach notification.

ANSPDCP announced its first fine under the GDPR, against UniCredit Bank S.A., after an investigation concluded on 27 June 2019. The bank had not applied adequate technical and organisational measures (data protection by design, data minimisation), so transaction detail documents made available online to payment beneficiaries disclosed the payer's national ID number (CNP) and address. 337,042 data subjects were affected between 25 May 2018 and 10 December 2018. The bank was fined RON 613,912, equivalent to EUR 130,000.

A Budapest police officer lost a private, unprotected USB stick holding personal data of the force's whole staff of about 1,733 people (birth data, mother's name, social security number, post). The police headquarters learned of the loss on 11 January 2019 but only notified the authority by post on 25 February 2019, well beyond the 72 hours. The authority found a breach of Article 33(1) GDPR, fined the headquarters HUF 5,000,000, ordered it to take measures so future breaches are notified on time, and ordered publication of the decision with the controller's identity.

A news article reports that the Spanish data protection authority fined LaLiga EUR 250,000 over its mobile app, which could remotely activate users' phone microphones to detect bars showing football without paying. The AEPD found the information given to users opaque and held that users must be informed each time the microphone is activated, not only at installation. It also found a breach of the requirement that consent can be withdrawn at any time. The authority gave LaLiga one month to correct the app. LaLiga disputes the findings and says it will appeal in court.
